items.why: Clearly distinguishes the five men taking the objects from the priest and soldiers standing outside.
Tests the order of two distinct transfers of the same objects, with a clear first event.
The trees are clearly asking for their own king, but 'Whose ruler' is awkward phrasing.
The excerpt gives a clear cause of prosperity, readily paraphrased as having everything they need.
Clearly asks readers to connect the search for a home with not yet receiving their own land.
The reason is explicit and unambiguous, though answering requires little beyond retrieving one clause.
Meaningfully distinguishes the relatives receiving instructions from the citizens who will receive the message.
Clearly distinguishes his stated purpose for leaving from the place he happens to reach.
Calls a conditional blessing a 'request' and mainly tests sentence order.
'Does something' and 'the report' make a simple question about the Levite unnecessarily vague and artificial.
The report concerns people going into the fields, but the competing answer can describe the same departure.
Usefully distinguishes whom the mother names as maker from who actually makes the image.
Readers can identify the unnamed victim as Abimelek by connecting the killing with the final sentence.
Requires connecting the burning stronghold with the deaths of the people sheltering inside.
Clearly distinguishes the endpoint of the priests' service from the separate period of idol use.
Shouting is the nearest cue, but being overtaken could also explain why the Danites turn.
Requires interpreting the rhetorical question as reluctance to sacrifice producing good fruit for power.
Burning is the stated immediate purpose, although attacking the tower is also a true, broader answer.
Readers must connect 'take it over' with the land rather than the people mentioned afterward.
Asks for Micah's stated reasoning and clearly distinguishes the priest's new role from his birthplace.
Awkward wording treats the region containing Micah's house as a separate preceding stop.
Tests a meaningful pronoun connection; either Jerub-Baal or the speaker's father identifies the right person.
The sender is clearly named, but this is mostly straightforward retrieval rather than deeper comprehension.
Meaningfully distinguishes the priest receiving the request from God, whom the priest is asked to consult.
Treats the curse as a later event, although the excerpt presents it as a summary of God's punishment.
The contrast is recoverable, but 'they' and the passive wording make the question unnecessarily indirect.
The intended result is explicit, but 'For what result' is an unnatural way to ask about it.
Requires interpreting the rhetorical question and explaining the tradeoff between useful oil and ruling.
Tests who uttered the reported curse rather than simply who speaks the surrounding quotation.
Clearly distinguishes the activity during the cursing from the earlier grape harvesting and processing.
Calls for a complete causal explanation combining distance from Sidon with lack of ties to others.
